## TL;DR

This round fixed three review findings around native browser captures, Docker failure classification, and old Hetzner runner snapshots. Native capture worktrees now live under the per-run checkout and are removed with it. Docker startup and cache preparation failures retain the reserved infrastructure exit codes, while project commands that exit 126 or 127 remain gate failures. Hetzner now probes the installed runner script for project-command support before uploading a bundle, and returns a clear update instruction when an old snapshot would otherwise run the stock Bun gate.

The changed-path check passed on ThinkPad, including 566 selected test files, the UI smoke test, and rendered contrast checks. Local format, lint, build, and remaining applicable guards also passed. The new focused Docker and native capture tests passed. No live Tiao Android/Gradle or real Hetzner snapshot execution was performed.

## Work and rationale

The native runner previously placed browser capture worktrees under a stable `$HOME/.repoos-worktrees/<branch>` path. Its EXIT trap removed only the per-run checkout and bundle, leaving the linked worktree and `node_modules` behind. A later capture of the same branch could fail because that branch already existed. The capture worktree now lives under `$WORK/worktrees`, so the existing cleanup removes the worktree and its installed files with the run. The test runs two captures of the same branch and confirms neither leaves a persistent home-directory worktree.

The Docker command branch already uses the gate-start marker to distinguish an exit 4 before the project gate begins. The review found that 125, 126, and 127 were still mapped to Docker startup failure even when they came from the project command, and that creating or preparing the cache volume was unguarded under `set -e`. The runner now checks for the marker before applying Docker's 125/126/127 startup mapping. Cache volume creation and root preparation each have an explicit failure message and map to exit 5. The existing gate marker is written to the artifact log before the project command starts, allowing a project command returning 126 or 127 to retain a gate-exit marker and be classified as a test failure.

The native capture setup had the same boundary issue: `bun install --frozen-lockfile || exit 4` could be followed by an unconditional gate-exit marker. The native script now writes the start marker only after capture dependencies install, or immediately before starting a configured project command. A pre-gate exit 4 is reported as setup failure. Its test exercises successful repeated captures and commits an invalid package manifest for a setup-failure run to verify that the failure has no gate marker.

Hetzner reused a mirror-capability probe but did not check whether its runner script understood `remoteValidation.command`. An older VM snapshot could therefore receive a command environment variable it ignored and run the stock Bun sequence instead. The probe now returns both mirror and command capability markers, caches both per VM, and refuses to upload/run a custom command if its script lacks support. The returned detail names the host, identifies `remoteValidation.command`, and includes the runner script update command. A regression test simulates an old script and verifies that validation stops after the capability probe, before any bundle upload or stock gate.

## Approaches tried

For the Docker result contract, the runner checks the artifact marker rather than relying on the numeric exit code alone. This preserves project-defined exit codes that overlap with Docker's startup codes. A fake Docker executable runs the actual `validate.sh` branch and verifies project exits 126/127, startup exit 127, cache-volume creation failure, and cache preparation failure. The image's explicit Bash entrypoint remains tested through captured argv and the successful fixture gate output.

For native capture cleanup, putting the linked checkout under `$WORK` makes cleanup follow the lifetime of the existing per-run trap; a separate persistent cleanup registry is unnecessary. For Hetzner, mirror and command capabilities share one small probe so a custom command does not add another network round trip on a new VM.

## Challenges and blockers

The first native capture test used a fake Bun executable, but the native script deliberately prepends `/opt/homebrew/bin` to PATH, so the host's real Bun took precedence. I replaced that fake with a minimal fixture package and a real Bun install; an invalid package manifest reliably exercises the pre-gate failure path. Focused tests then passed. The full changed-path check takes several minutes; I waited for the remote and local portions to finish.

The tests run with fixture repositories, fake Docker, and an injected Hetzner SSH result. They do not prove a live Android SDK setup, a real cloud snapshot update, or routing across actual hosts. Those environments were unavailable during this session.

## Key learnings

Per-run filesystem ownership is simpler and safer when all temporary worktrees are created under the run's cleanup root. Exit codes alone cannot distinguish an infrastructure failure from a project command that intentionally returns the same number; a persisted gate-start marker must guard every reserved-code remap. Finally, script compatibility must be checked for every provider path: a pool's health probe did not protect the separate Hetzner VM path, even though both use the same runner script contract.
